title: How do you add gRPC-web browser support (Envoy proxy translating HTTP/1.1 ↔ HTTP/2)?
shortTitle: How do you add gRPC-web browser support (Envoy proxy translating HTTP/1.1 ↔ HTTP/2)?

s1_definition.profdef: gRPC-Web is a variant of gRPC that lets browser JavaScript call a gRPC backend, because browsers cannot speak raw gRPC over HTTP/2 (they have no low-level control over HTTP/2 frames and trailers). A browser sends a gRPC-Web request over ordinary HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, and a proxy such as Envoy translates between the gRPC-Web wire format and native gRPC over HTTP/2, forwarding to the backend. Envoy's `grpc_web` filter does this translation, so the backend stays pure gRPC while the browser uses a gRPC-Web client stub.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India's internal departments speak a fast shorthand code (native gRPC over HTTP/2) that only trained staff understand. A customer at the public web counter (the browser) only speaks plain language (HTTP/1.1). So the bank places a translator at the front desk (Envoy proxy) who takes the customer's plain request, rewrites it into the internal shorthand, hands it to the back office, and translates the reply back. The back office never changes how it works, and the customer never needs to learn the shorthand.
s1_definition.oneliner: gRPC-Web lets browsers call gRPC services, and Envoy's grpc_web filter translates the browser's gRPC-Web calls into native gRPC over HTTP/2 for the backend.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** gRPC-Web is a variant of gRPC that lets browser JavaScript call a gRPC backend, because browsers cannot speak raw gRPC over HTTP/2 (they have no low-level control over HTTP/2 frames and trailers). A browser sends a gRPC-Web request over ordinary HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, and a proxy such as Envoy translates between the gRPC-Web wire format and native gRPC over HTTP/2, forwarding to the backend. Envoy's `grpc_web` filter does this translation, so the backend stays pure gRPC while the browser uses a gRPC-Web client stub.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India's internal departments speak a fast shorthand code (native gRPC over HTTP/2) that only trained staff understand. A customer at the public web counter (the browser) only speaks plain language (HTTP/1.1). So the bank places a translator at the front desk (Envoy proxy) who takes the customer's plain request, rewrites it into the internal shorthand, hands it to the back office, and translates the reply back. The back office never changes how it works, and the customer never needs to learn the shorthand.

**One line to remember:** gRPC-Web lets browsers call gRPC services, and Envoy's grpc_web filter translates the browser's gRPC-Web calls into native gRPC over HTTP/2 for the backend.

sections.s2_technical:
The core problem is that the browser fetch and XHR APIs do not expose HTTP/2 trailers or framing control, and native gRPC depends on HTTP/2 trailers to carry the final status. gRPC-Web defines a slightly different wire format that packs the status into the response body so a browser can read it over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. You cannot point a browser at a native gRPC server directly; you need a translating proxy in between.

Envoy is the most common proxy. You configure an Envoy listener with an HTTP connection manager, add the `envoy.filters.http.grpc_web` filter, and route to an upstream cluster that uses HTTP/2 to talk to your gRPC backend. The `grpc_web` filter unwraps the gRPC-Web framing and re-emits a native gRPC request upstream, then wraps the native gRPC response (including trailers) back into gRPC-Web for the browser. You also usually add a CORS filter because the browser enforces cross-origin rules.

On the browser side you generate gRPC-Web stubs with `protoc` using the `grpc-web` plugin, choosing a mode such as `grpcwebtext` or `grpcweb` (binary). Your JavaScript then calls `client.transfer(request, metadata, callback)` just like a normal gRPC stub, and the stub handles the gRPC-Web framing. A senior nuance: gRPC-Web supports unary and server streaming, but it does not support client streaming or bidirectional streaming today, because the browser still cannot stream a request body frame by frame. Another nuance is that in Spring Boot you can alternatively use the built-in gRPC-Web support in some starters, but in production a dedicated Envoy sidecar or edge proxy is the standard, because it also gives you TLS termination, load balancing, and observability in one place.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India already runs a pure gRPC account service for internal calls, and now the new web dashboard written in JavaScript must show Rajesh his balance. The browser simply cannot open a native gRPC call because it has no access to HTTP/2 trailers. This is exactly what gRPC-Web solves — a browser-friendly framing for gRPC.

Problem 2 — The bank does not want to rewrite the backend or maintain a separate REST layer just for the browser. This is exactly what Envoy's grpc_web filter solves — it sits in front and translates, so the backend stays pure gRPC and the browser gets a stub that feels native.

The demo shows the account.proto contract, a pure gRPC server implementation, the Envoy configuration with the grpc_web and CORS filters, and a small Java gateway-style client that mimics what the translated request reaches on the backend. Classes and steps: `account.proto` (contract), `BalanceServiceImpl` (pure gRPC server), `envoy.yaml` (translation config), and `BalanceClient` (represents the call that lands on the backend after translation).

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the pure gRPC backend
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Start the backend (native gRPC on 9090)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.grpcweb.GrpcServer

# Start Envoy (browser-facing on 8080, translates gRPC-Web ↔ gRPC)
docker run --rm --network host -v $(pwd)/envoy.yaml:/etc/envoy/envoy.yaml envoyproxy/envoy:v1.29-latest

# Generate browser stubs (what the JS dashboard uses)
protoc -I=src/main/proto account.proto \
  --js_out=import_style=commonjs:./web \
  --grpc-web_out=import_style=commonjs,mode=grpcwebtext:./web

# Verify backend directly (post-translation path)
java -cp target/classes com.bank.grpcweb.BalanceClient
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the web dashboard asks for the balance of Rajesh (SAV2001).

Step 1 — The browser's generated gRPC-Web stub builds a `BalanceRequest`, serializes it in the gRPC-Web framing, and sends it over HTTP/1.1 to Envoy on port 8080. The browser cannot use native gRPC because it has no access to HTTP/2 trailers.

Step 2 — Envoy's grpc_web filter receives the request, unwraps the gRPC-Web framing, and re-emits a native gRPC request over HTTP/2 to the backend on port 9090. The CORS filter has already allowed the cross-origin call.

Step 3 — `BalanceServiceImpl.getBalance` runs as a normal gRPC method, finds Rajesh with balance Rs.1,000,000, and returns a `BalanceResponse` plus the trailing gRPC status over HTTP/2.

Step 4 — Envoy wraps the native gRPC response, including the status that was in HTTP/2 trailers, back into the gRPC-Web body format, and sends it to the browser over HTTP/1.1. The browser stub decodes it and the dashboard shows Rajesh's balance. The backend never knew a browser was involved.

```
2026-10-26 15:05:01 [INFO] Pure gRPC BalanceService on 9090 (Envoy on 8080 for browsers)
2026-10-26 15:05:03 [INFO] gRPC-Web GetBalance for SAV2001
2026-10-26 15:05:03 [INFO] Holder=Rajesh Balance=Rs.1000000
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Browser JS (grpc-web stub)
    │ BalanceRequest → gRPC-Web framing (status in body)
    ▼ HTTP/1.1  (CORS preflight first)
  Envoy :8080  [envoy.filters.http.grpc_web + cors]
    │ unwrap gRPC-Web → native gRPC
    ▼ HTTP/2 (http2_protocol_options)
  BalanceServiceImpl.getBalance(req, obs)  :9090
    │ lookup SAV2001 → Rajesh, Rs.1,000,000
    │ obs.onNext(BalanceResponse) ; obs.onCompleted()  (status in HTTP/2 trailer)
    ▲ HTTP/2 response + trailer
  Envoy  wrap native gRPC → gRPC-Web (status back into body)
    ▲ HTTP/1.1
  Browser decodes → dashboard shows Rs.1,000,000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — gRPC-Web Translation Design ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Adapter/Translator: Envoy adapts gRPC-Web ↔ native gRPC        │
  │    WHY: browser cannot speak HTTP/2 trailers; backend stays pure│
  │ Proxy: Envoy front-proxy terminates and forwards               │
  │    WHY: one place for TLS, CORS, routing, observability         │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: BalanceServiceImpl only serves balances; Envoy only routes  │
  │ O: add new rpc = extend proto; proxy config unchanged          │
  │ D: browser depends on generated stub, not on transport details │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Supported Call Kinds over gRPC-Web (as prose) ─────────────
  unary          : supported  (GetBalance)
  server-stream  : supported  (statement feed)
  client-stream  : NOT supported in browser
  bidi-stream    : NOT supported in browser

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. browser stub.getBalance(req) → gRPC-Web over HTTP/1.1
  2.   → Envoy grpc_web filter unwraps → native gRPC over HTTP/2
  3.   → BalanceServiceImpl.getBalance(req, obs)
  4.   → obs.onNext/onCompleted → HTTP/2 trailer status
  5.   → Envoy rewraps → gRPC-Web body → browser decodes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The reason browsers need gRPC-Web is that native gRPC depends on HTTP/2 trailers to carry the final call status, and browser networking APIs like fetch and XHR do not give you access to HTTP/2 trailers or frame-level control. So Google defined gRPC-Web, a slightly different wire format that packs the status into the response body, and a browser-generated gRPC-Web stub speaks that format over ordinary HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. But the backend is still pure gRPC, so you put a translating proxy in the middle.

Envoy is the standard proxy for this. I configure an HTTP connection manager with the grpc_web filter and a CORS filter, and I route to an upstream cluster that is forced to use HTTP/2 so it can speak native gRPC to the backend. The grpc_web filter unwraps the browser's gRPC-Web request into native gRPC on the way in, and wraps the native gRPC response, including the trailer status, back into gRPC-Web on the way out. The CORS filter is needed because the browser enforces cross-origin rules and does a preflight request first.

In my banking work at National Bank of India we already had a pure gRPC balance service for internal calls, and when the new JavaScript dashboard needed to show Rajesh his balance, we did not rewrite the backend or build a parallel REST layer. We generated a gRPC-Web stub with the grpc-web protoc plugin, put an Envoy proxy in front, and the dashboard called getBalance as if it were a normal gRPC call. The backend never knew a browser was on the other end.

The senior detail I always add is the limitation: gRPC-Web supports unary and server streaming, but it does not support client streaming or bidirectional streaming, because the browser still cannot stream a request body frame by frame. I also mention that in production the Envoy proxy is doing double duty, giving us TLS termination, load balancing, and observability in the same hop, which is why a dedicated proxy is preferred over embedding translation inside the application.
